resources.string: Broken algorithms (DES, RC4), reused IVs, ECB mode, weak padding, insufficient key length, or XOR/Base64 passed off as encryption.
Data encrypted with AES-256-GCM. NIST-approved, authenticated, and computationally infeasible to break.
Data encrypted with DES — key is only 56-bit, broken since 1999. Brute-forced in under 24 hours with modern hardware.
AES-GCM used — each block is unique, authenticated, and indistinguishable from random.
AES/ECB used — identical plaintext blocks produce identical ciphertext blocks. Data patterns fully visible in ciphertext.
256-bit AES key. Provides 128-bit security strength — infeasible to brute-force.
64-bit AES key used — far below the 128-bit minimum. Brute-forceable with modern hardware.
Separate keys generated for encryption and signing. Key separation enforced per NIST SP 800-57.
Same RSA key used for both encryption and signing. Cross-protocol attacks can break one use case using the other.
Real AES-256-GCM encryption with Keystore-backed key. Not reversible without the key.
Data "encrypted" with XOR and encoded as Base64. Trivially reversible — provides zero security.
Fresh random 16-byte IV generated via SecureRandom for every encryption. IV prepended to ciphertext.
IV hardcoded to all-zeros. Two ciphertexts encrypted with the same key+IV reveal XOR of plaintexts — full plaintext recovery possible.
AES-GCM authenticates ciphertext before decryption. Padding oracle attacks are impossible.
AES/CBC/PKCS5Padding with observable error response. 128 requests per byte — full plaintext recoverable via padding oracle attack.
